whyWrongByChoice.D: Replication errors change sequence, not the circular shape of the chromosome.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Plasmids replicate independently and are retained and even shared between bacteria.

questions.stem: A previously healthy college student develops fever, neck stiffness, and confusion and deteriorates over the course of a single day. Which of the following features of bacterial infection does this course best illustrate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bacteria cause permanent damage only after months without treatment

choices.label: B
choices.text: Bacteria grow slowly and cause disease only after several weeks

choices.label: C
choices.text: Bacteria must undergo conjugation before they can become virulent

choices.label: D
choices.text: Bacteria replicate rapidly and can overwhelm a host within hours

choices.label: E
choices.text: Bacteria require a viral coinfection in order to invade the meninges

explanation.summary: Rapid bacterial replication lets some infections, such as bacterial meningitis, overwhelm a patient within a day.
explanation.whyCorrect: Because of their rapid replication, some bacteria can quickly overwhelm a patient before the illness is even recognized as severe. In some cases of bacterial meningitis, the time from the start of symptoms to death is less than 24 hours, and survivors commonly suffer amputations from sepsis or permanent neurologic damage. Vaccines are used to prevent some of these rare but extremely aggressive infections.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Amputations and permanent neurologic damage follow even acutely treated infections.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Rapid division allows some bacterial infections to become lethal within a single day.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Conjugation spreads plasmid-borne resistance; it is not a prerequisite for virulence.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Bacterial meningitis does not require a preceding or concurrent viral infection.

questions.stem: A resistance gene is found at a different chromosomal location in a daughter colony than in the parent colony, while the sequence of the gene itself is unchanged. Which genetic element most likely accounts for this?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A 30S subunit bound to the gene

choices.label: B
choices.text: A point mutation within the gene

choices.label: C
choices.text: A prophage dormant in the chromosome

choices.label: D
choices.text: A sex pilus extending from the cell

choices.label: E
choices.text: A transposon flanking the gene

explanation.summary: Transposons are DNA sequences with enzyme-coding genes that let DNA jump to new sites within a genome.
explanation.whyCorrect: Transposons are DNA sequences that contain enzyme-coding genes allowing transposition of DNA sequences within a genome. In bacteria they let sequences jump around the genome and between plasmids and chromosomal DNA, often carrying drug-resistance genes with them. Because the enzyme cleaves and ligates at the transposon sequence, the gene of interest is left intact at its new location.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The 30S subunit is part of the protein-synthesis machinery and does not bind or relocate genes.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A point mutation would alter the gene sequence rather than relocate it unchanged.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A prophage is integrated viral DNA lying dormant; it does not shuttle host genes around the chromosome.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The sex pilus forms the mating bridge between two cells in conjugation; it does not move genes within a genome.

questions.stem: A gene encoding β-lactamase is to be moved from the bacterial chromosome onto a plasmid by transposition. Which of the following conditions must be met for the intact gene to be relocated?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A prophage must be integrated immediately next to the gene

choices.label: B
choices.text: A transposon sequence must flank both sides of the gene

choices.label: C
choices.text: A transposon sequence must lie on one side of the gene only

choices.label: D
choices.text: The gene must be positioned at the origin of replication

choices.label: E
choices.text: The gene must first be converted into single-stranded DNA

explanation.summary: Transposition carries a gene only when transposon sequences flank both sides of it.
explanation.whyCorrect: A transposon sequence must flank both sides of the gene of interest, because the transposon-encoded enzyme cleaves and ligates at the transposon sequences themselves. Cutting at both flanks releases the whole gene and leaves the gene of interest intact. This is how a chromosomal β-lactamase gene can be transposed onto a plasmid for subsequent transfer by conjugation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Prophage integration underlies specialized transduction, which is a different transfer mechanism.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cleavage occurs at the transposon sequence, so a single flank cannot excise the whole gene intact.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Position relative to the origin determines transfer order in Hfr conjugation, not transposition.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Transposition relocates double-stranded DNA; strand separation is not required.

questions.stem: Transposons carried by a bacterium are best described as performing which of the following functions?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Degrading β-lactam antibiotics before they reach the cell wall target

choices.label: B
choices.text: Forming the physical bridge across which a plasmid passes between two cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: Packaging fragments of host bacterial DNA into the capsid of a bacteriophage

choices.label: D
choices.text: Relocating DNA sequences within the genome and between plasmid and chromosome

choices.label: E
choices.text: Taking up naked DNA released into the environment by dying or lysed cells

explanation.summary: Transposons move DNA sequences around the genome and between plasmid and chromosomal DNA.
explanation.whyCorrect: In bacteria, transposons allow DNA sequences to jump around the genome as well as between plasmids and chromosomal DNA, often carrying drug-resistance sequences with them. This is how a resistance gene acquired on a plasmid can end up in the recipient's chromosomal DNA, so that all future progeny of that bacterium carry it.

whyWrongByChoice.A: That is the action of the enzyme β-lactamase, not of a mobile DNA element.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The mating bridge is formed by the sex pilus encoded by the F plasmid.
whyWrongByChoice.C: That describes generalized transduction, carried out by a lytic bacteriophage.
whyWrongByChoice.E: That describes transformation, performed by competent bacteria.

questions.stem: A patient with an Escherichia coli infection is treated with ampicillin. This drug exerts its antibacterial effect through which of the following mechanisms?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Binding bacterial helicase and preventing unwinding at the origin

choices.label: B
choices.text: Binding penicillin-binding proteins and blocking wall cross-linking

choices.label: C
choices.text: Binding the 30S ribosomal subunit and halting protein production

choices.label: D
choices.text: Binding the 50S ribosomal subunit and halting peptide elongation

choices.label: E
choices.text: Binding the sex pilus and preventing formation of a mating bridge

explanation.summary: β-lactams such as ampicillin bind penicillin-binding proteins and prevent cross-linking of the peptidoglycan cell wall.
explanation.whyCorrect: Ampicillin, amoxicillin, and piperacillin are β-lactam antibiotics used to treat gram-positive more than gram-negative infections. They function by binding to penicillin-binding proteins on bacteria and preventing cross-linking of the peptidoglycan cell wall. Resistance arises when a bacterium acquires β-lactamase, which binds and degrades the penicillin molecules.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Helicase is a replication enzyme and is not inhibited by β-lactam antibiotics.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The 30S subunit is the target of tetracyclines such as doxycycline.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Agents binding the 50S subunit also act on the ribosome rather than on the cell wall.
whyWrongByChoice.E: No β-lactam works by blocking conjugation or pilus function.

questions.stem: An Escherichia coli isolate is unaffected by ampicillin because it produces an enzyme that binds penicillin molecules and degrades them. This enzyme is which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: DNA polymerase III

choices.label: B
choices.text: Helicase

choices.label: C
choices.text: Penicillin-binding protein

choices.label: D
choices.text: Transposase

choices.label: E
choices.text: β-lactamase

explanation.summary: β-lactamase binds and degrades penicillin molecules, conferring resistance to β-lactam antibiotics.
explanation.whyCorrect: Under the selective pressure of antibiotic exposure, a rapidly dividing E. coli population may include a cell carrying a gene encoding β-lactamase. That enzyme binds penicillin molecules, degrades them, and provides the bacterium with resistance to these antibiotics. The gene can then be transposed onto a plasmid and shared with other bacteria.

whyWrongByChoice.A: DNA polymerase III synthesizes and proofreads the daughter DNA strand.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Helicase unwinds the chromosome at the origin of replication.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Penicillin-binding proteins are the bacterial target of the drug, not the resistance enzyme.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Transposase-type enzymes cleave and ligate at transposon sequences to relocate genes.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman with cystitis has taken trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for 4 days with no change in her burning and urgency. Urine culture grows more than 100,000 CFU/mL of Escherichia coli that is resistant to trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and susceptible to fluoroquinolones. Which of the following best explains her persistent symptoms?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Four days is too early for any antimicrobial agent to relieve cystitis symptoms

choices.label: B
choices.text: The culture result reflects specimen contamination rather than true infection

choices.label: C
choices.text: The infecting organism carries a determinant that inactivates the prescribed drug

choices.label: D
choices.text: The organism has not yet reached the colony count required to cause symptoms

choices.label: E
choices.text: The urinary tract is inaccessible to orally administered antimicrobial agents

explanation.summary: Treatment failure here reflects acquired resistance in the infecting organism, confirmed by sensitivity testing.
explanation.whyCorrect: The culture is positive for more than 100,000 CFU of E. coli, an organism usually treated with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, but sensitivity results show the isolate is resistant to that drug and sensitive to fluoroquinolones. Resistance genes of this kind are acquired and shared through plasmids, transposons, and horizontal gene transfer under antibiotic selective pressure. Switching to an agent shown to work against the isolate should bring improvement within 36 to 48 hours.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Improvement is expected within about 36 to 48 hours once an effective drug is given.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A single organism at this colony count in a symptomatic patient represents true infection.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A count above 100,000 CFU/mL already represents a heavy, symptomatic infection.
whyWrongByChoice.E: These agents reach the urinary tract well, and a susceptible isolate would be expected to respond.

questions.stem: A febrile, hypotensive patient is started on broad-spectrum piperacillin-tazobactam before an organism is identified, in order to keep the infection from progressing to sepsis. Which of the following is the principal population-level risk created by widespread use of this practice?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Blockade of conjugation between bacteria in the patient's gut

choices.label: B
choices.text: Conversion of the patient's normal flora into competent bacteria

choices.label: C
choices.text: Loss of resistance plasmids from the treated bacterial population

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reversal of mutations already present in the infecting organism

choices.label: E
choices.text: Selection of resistant organisms under antibiotic selective pressure

explanation.summary: Repeated broad-spectrum exposure selects out resistant organisms, the same natural-selection process that creates superbugs.
explanation.whyCorrect: Empirical broad-spectrum therapy is used to prevent progression to sepsis while the work-up continues. However, commonplace use of broad-spectrum antibiotics can lead to formation of superbugs with antibiotic resistance that are selected out through the concept of natural selection when bacteria are repeatedly exposed to antibiotics.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Antibiotics do not interrupt conjugation, and resistance plasmids continue to spread.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Competence is an intrinsic property of certain species, not something antibiotics confer.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Antibiotic exposure favors retention and spread of resistance plasmids rather than their loss.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Antibiotics select among variants already present; they do not reverse mutations.

questions.stem: Bacteria obtain new fragments of DNA from other bacteria through horizontal gene transfer. Which of the following is the most common mechanism of horizontal gene transfer?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Binary fission

choices.label: B
choices.text: Conjugation

choices.label: C
choices.text: Transcription

choices.label: D
choices.text: Transduction

choices.label: E
choices.text: Transformation

explanation.summary: Conjugation is the most common of the three horizontal gene transfer mechanisms.
explanation.whyCorrect: The three mechanisms of horizontal gene transfer are conjugation, transformation, and transduction. The most common mechanism is conjugation, which is also the one that most resembles what people imagine when they think of bacteria mating. Through these mechanisms bacteria evolve, spreading antibiotic resistance and immune evasion.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Binary fission is clonal division of a single cell, not transfer between cells.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Transcription produces RNA from DNA within one cell and transfers nothing.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Transduction is the least common of the three mechanisms.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Transformation does occur, but less commonly than conjugation.

questions.stem: The three mechanisms of horizontal gene transfer are compared in a bacterial population. Which of the following correctly ranks them from most common to least common?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Conjugation, transduction, transformation

choices.label: B
choices.text: Conjugation, transformation, transduction

choices.label: C
choices.text: Transduction, transformation, conjugation

choices.label: D
choices.text: Transformation, conjugation, transduction

choices.label: E
choices.text: Transformation, transduction, conjugation

explanation.summary: Conjugation is most common, followed by transformation, with transduction least common.
explanation.whyCorrect: Conjugation is the most common horizontal gene transfer mechanism. The other two occur less commonly, with transformation occurring more often than transduction. The correct ordering is therefore conjugation, then transformation, then transduction.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Transformation occurs more often than transduction, so the last two are reversed here.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Transduction is the least common mechanism, so it cannot be listed first.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Conjugation, not transformation, is the most common mechanism.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Conjugation is the most common mechanism and cannot be listed last.

questions.stem: A resistance determinant first identified in a Klebsiella isolate is later recovered from an unrelated gram-negative genus on the same hospital unit. Which of the following statements about horizontal gene transfer is best supported?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It can occur between bacteria of different genera

choices.label: B
choices.text: It occurs only between bacteria and human host cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: It occurs only between two cells of one identical strain

choices.label: D
choices.text: It occurs only during binary fission of the donor cell

choices.label: E
choices.text: It occurs only when both cells are already resistant

explanation.summary: Horizontal gene transfer occurs within a species and, for some bacteria, even between different genera.
explanation.whyCorrect: Horizontal gene transfer mechanisms operate not only within the same species of bacteria; some bacteria are even capable of obtaining DNA from different genera. This is why a resistance determinant can appear in an unrelated genus sharing the same environment, allowing an adaptation such as antibiotic resistance to spread across a bacterial population.

whyWrongByChoice.B: These mechanisms move DNA between bacteria, not from bacteria into human cells.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Transfer occurs within a species and, for some organisms, across species and genera.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The transfer mechanisms are distinct from division of the donor cell.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The point of transfer is that a susceptible recipient acquires resistance it lacked.

questions.stem: A bacterial strain is unable to act as a donor in conjugation because it cannot produce a sex pilus. Absence of which of the following best explains this?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A capsid

choices.label: B
choices.text: A prophage

choices.label: C
choices.text: A transposon

choices.label: D
choices.text: Competence

choices.label: E
choices.text: The F plasmid

explanation.summary: Only bacteria carrying the F plasmid, which encodes the sex pilus, can serve as conjugation donors.
explanation.whyCorrect: Only bacteria with the F plasmid are able to undergo conjugation as donors. The F plasmid contains DNA that encodes production of a sex pilus, and that pilus connects the F+ bacterium to an F- bacterium to form the mating bridge. A cell lacking the F plasmid is F- and can only receive.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The capsid is the protein coat of a bacteriophage, not a bacterial structure.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A prophage is integrated phage DNA and underlies specialized transduction, not pilus formation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Transposons relocate genes within a genome and do not build surface appendages.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Competence permits uptake of naked DNA in transformation, a separate mechanism.

questions.stem: An F+ Escherichia coli forms a mating bridge with an F- cell, and conjugation proceeds to completion. Which of the following best describes the outcome?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Both cells end with a double-stranded F plasmid and are F+

choices.label: B
choices.text: Both cells end with a plasmid plus a copy of the donor chromosome

choices.label: C
choices.text: The donor becomes F- while the recipient also remains F-

choices.label: D
choices.text: The recipient gains a fragment of donor chromosome and stays F-

choices.label: E
choices.text: The recipient keeps the transferred plasmid as single-stranded DNA

explanation.summary: In F+ x F- conjugation a single plasmid strand crosses the bridge and both cells finish as F+.
explanation.whyCorrect: A single strand of the double-stranded F plasmid is transferred across the mating bridge, beginning at the origin of the plasmid, and no chromosomal DNA is transferred. Following transfer, each bacterium synthesizes the necessary complementary strand, restoring a double-stranded plasmid in both cells. Both the donor and the former recipient are therefore F+.

whyWrongByChoice.B: F+ x F- conjugation transfers no chromosomal DNA at all.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The donor retains its plasmid and the recipient gains one, so neither cell ends F-.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Transfer of flanking chromosomal DNA leaving the recipient F- describes Hfr conjugation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Each cell synthesizes the complementary strand after transfer, restoring double-stranded DNA.

questions.stem: During conjugation, a donor strain transfers a fragment of its own chromosome to the recipient, and the recipient does not itself become a donor. Which of the following best describes this donor strain?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A cell carrying a free F plasmid that is separate from its chromosome

choices.label: B
choices.text: A cell lysogenized by a temperate phage at a chromosomal insertion site

choices.label: C
choices.text: A cell that has lost its F plasmid and has become an F- recipient

choices.label: D
choices.text: A cell that has taken up naked chromosomal DNA from its environment

choices.label: E
choices.text: A cell whose F plasmid is integrated into its own chromosomal DNA

explanation.summary: Hfr strains carry the F plasmid integrated into the chromosome, so conjugation drags flanking chromosomal DNA along.
explanation.whyCorrect: High-frequency recombination (Hfr) strains contain the F plasmid within the chromosomal DNA, usually integrated through site-specific recombination at insertion sites. Transfer starts at the origin in the F plasmid sequence, and because the plasmid is incorporated into the chromosome, flanking chromosomal DNA is carried across as well. Generally only a fragment of the donor chromosome is transferred, so the recipient becomes a recombinant F- cell rather than a donor.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A free F plasmid gives F+ x F- conjugation, which transfers no chromosomal DNA and makes the recipient F+.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A lysogen carries prophage DNA, which supports specialized transduction rather than conjugation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: An F- cell cannot make a sex pilus and therefore cannot act as the donor.
whyWrongByChoice.D: That describes a transformed cell, and transformation does not use a mating bridge.

questions.stem: In an experiment, conjugating bacterial pairs are agitated to break the mating bridge at successive time points, and the recipients are then tested for donor genes. Which of the following results is expected?

choices.label: A
choices.text: All donor genes appear in the recipient regardless of interruption time

choices.label: B
choices.text: Donor genes appear only when the bridge is broken in the first minute

choices.label: C
choices.text: Genes closest to the origin of transfer appear in the recipient first

choices.label: D
choices.text: Genes farthest from the origin of transfer appear in the recipient first

choices.label: E
choices.text: No donor genes appear because interrupted transfer is always aborted

explanation.summary: Interrupting conjugation gives the recipient only origin-proximal donor genes, which allows gene order to be mapped.
explanation.whyCorrect: Bacterial conjugation can be interrupted if the mating bridge breaks before DNA transfer is complete, so the recipient receives only part of the donor DNA. Because transfer begins at the origin, only the genes closest to the origin of transfer are given to the recipient when the bridge breaks early. Varying the interruption time therefore reveals gene order and is useful for experimental mapping.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Breaking the bridge early prevents full transfer, so only part of the donor DNA arrives.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Earlier interruption transfers less DNA, not more.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Transfer starts at the origin, so origin-proximal genes arrive earliest, not last.
whyWrongByChoice.E: DNA that crossed before the break is retained, which is what makes the technique informative.

questions.stem: A bacterium takes up a fragment of DNA released into its surroundings by neighboring cells that have died and lysed. This process is called which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Binary fission

choices.label: B
choices.text: Conjugation

choices.label: C
choices.text: Transduction

choices.label: D
choices.text: Transformation

choices.label: E
choices.text: Transposition

explanation.summary: Transformation is uptake of naked DNA from the environment by a competent bacterium.
explanation.whyCorrect: Transformation is the taking up of naked DNA from the environment, and that naked DNA usually comes from dying or lysed cells. Bacteria capable of transformation are described as competent. The absorbed DNA is then incorporated into the host chromosome through homologous recombination.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Binary fission is division of one cell into two clones of itself.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Conjugation requires physical contact and a mating bridge between two living cells.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Transduction requires a bacteriophage to carry the DNA into the recipient.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Transposition relocates DNA within a genome rather than importing it from outside.

questions.stem: Only certain bacteria are competent, meaning they are able to take up naked DNA from their environment. Which of the following organisms is competent?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bacteroides fragilis

choices.label: B
choices.text: Clostridium tetani

choices.label: C
choices.text: Mycobacterium tuberculosis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Streptococcus pneumoniae

choices.label: E
choices.text: Treponema pallidum

explanation.summary: Classic competent organisms include S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae type B, N. meningitidis, and E. coli.
explanation.whyCorrect: Bacteria capable of transformation are called competent, and the classic examples are Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae type B, Neisseria meningitidis, and Escherichia coli. These organisms can absorb naked DNA from lysed neighbors and incorporate it by homologous recombination, which is one route by which they acquire resistance and capsular genes.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Bacteroides fragilis is not among the classically competent organisms.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Clostridium tetani is not among the organisms classically described as naturally competent.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Mycobacterium tuberculosis is not among the classically competent organisms.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Treponema pallidum is not among the classically competent organisms.

questions.stem: Naked DNA taken up by a competent bacterium is incorporated into the recipient chromosome by homologous recombination. Which of the following conditions does this process require?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The donor DNA must be delivered inside a bacteriophage capsid

choices.label: B
choices.text: The donor DNA must be flanked on both sides by transposon sequences

choices.label: C
choices.text: The donor DNA must integrate at a specific chromosomal insertion site

choices.label: D
choices.text: The donor DNA must share similar nucleotide sequences with host DNA

choices.label: E
choices.text: The donor DNA must stay extrachromosomal and replicate on its own

explanation.summary: Homologous recombination requires the absorbed DNA and host DNA to have similar nucleotide sequences that can be exchanged.
explanation.whyCorrect: Implementation of absorbed DNA into the host bacterial chromosome occurs through homologous recombination, which requires the host DNA and the absorbed DNA to have similar nucleotide sequences that are then exchanged. Without that sequence similarity, the imported fragment cannot be swapped into the chromosome.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Naked DNA in transformation comes from dying or lysed cells rather than from a capsid.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Flanking transposon sequences are required for transposition, a different mechanism.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Integration at defined insertion sites describes site-specific recombination, as in Hfr formation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Incorporation into the host chromosome is exactly what homologous recombination achieves.

questions.stem: A bacteriophage attaches to surface receptors on a susceptible bacterium. Which of the following occurs next?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The phage delivers its capsid proteins and retains its nucleic acid

choices.label: B
choices.text: The phage fuses its envelope with the bacterial cytoplasmic membrane

choices.label: C
choices.text: The phage injects its nucleic acid while the capsid remains outside

choices.label: D
choices.text: The phage is drawn through a sex pilus and across a mating bridge

choices.label: E
choices.text: The whole phage particle is engulfed and dissolved in the cytoplasm

explanation.summary: A bacteriophage binds surface receptors and injects its DNA, leaving the protein capsid outside the cell.
explanation.whyCorrect: Viruses that infect bacteria are called bacteriophages. The phage infects a susceptible bacterial cell by binding on surface receptors and injecting its DNA into the host bacterial cell, while the rest of the phage, including the protein coat or capsid, remains on the outside of the bacterium. Most phages carry DNA encoding production of phage progeny, which ultimately lyses the infected cell.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The reverse is true: nucleic acid is delivered and the coat is left behind.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Phage entry occurs by receptor binding and DNA injection, not by envelope fusion.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The sex pilus and mating bridge belong to conjugation between two bacteria.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The protein coat stays outside the bacterium; only nucleic acid enters.

questions.stem: During lytic growth in a donor bacterium, a phage particle is assembled around a random fragment of host chromosomal DNA instead of viral DNA. When this particle infects a new bacterium, which of the following occurs?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The delivered DNA consists of sequence adjacent to a former integration site

choices.label: B
choices.text: The delivered DNA integrates and lies dormant in the cell as a prophage

choices.label: C
choices.text: The delivered DNA is expressed and recombined into the recipient chromosome

choices.label: D
choices.text: The delivered DNA is retained only as a free, independent plasmid

choices.label: E
choices.text: The new cell is lysed as a fresh crop of phage progeny is assembled

explanation.summary: Generalized transduction packages random host DNA; the recipient expresses it and recombines it into its chromosome without being lysed.
explanation.whyCorrect: In generalized transduction, some phages produced during lytic growth are packaged with host bacterial DNA rather than viral DNA; these are the transducing phages. A bacterial cell infected by a transducing phage is not lysed, because the particle carries no viral DNA. Instead the donor bacterial DNA is expressed and swapped in through homologous recombination into the chromosome of the recipient progeny.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Transfer of DNA that flanked an integration site describes specialized transduction.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Prophage formation requires viral DNA from a temperate phage, which this particle lacks.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The incoming DNA is recombined into the recipient chromosome rather than kept as a plasmid.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Without viral DNA the particle cannot direct production of progeny or lyse the cell.

questions.stem: A temperate bacteriophage integrated in a bacterial chromosome undergoes induction, and its DNA is excised imprecisely. Which of the following describes the DNA that the resulting phage particles carry into a new recipient?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A complete copy of the donor chromosome along with its plasmids

choices.label: B
choices.text: A random fragment of the donor chromosome and no viral DNA at all

choices.label: C
choices.text: Naked donor DNA taken from the environment around a lysed cell

choices.label: D
choices.text: Only viral DNA, with no sequence at all from the donor bacterium

choices.label: E
choices.text: Viral DNA together with donor DNA that lay immediately adjacent

explanation.summary: Specialized transduction is an excisional process that carries viral DNA plus the host DNA immediately flanking the prophage.
explanation.whyCorrect: A temperate bacteriophage integrates its DNA into the host chromosome as a prophage, which remains dormant and is passed to child cells. When induction occurs, the prophage DNA is imprecisely excised and brings along the host bacterium's immediately adjacent DNA. The recipient's genome then includes its own DNA, the bacteriophage viral DNA, and specific DNA from the previous bacterial host, in contrast to the random DNA carried in generalized transduction.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Only the limited adjacent segment is carried, not the entire donor chromosome.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Random packaging of host DNA with no viral DNA defines generalized transduction.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Free DNA taken up from the environment is the substrate of transformation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Imprecise excision carries flanking bacterial sequence along with the viral genome.

questions.stem: A strain of Corynebacterium diphtheriae produces diphtheria toxin only after it has been infected by a particular bacteriophage. Which of the following best explains this observation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Binary fission of the phage generates toxin inside the cell

choices.label: B
choices.text: Competent bacteria take up toxin protein from the environment

choices.label: C
choices.text: Conjugation with the phage delivers a toxin-encoding plasmid

choices.label: D
choices.text: Temperate phages can carry DNA that encodes bacterial toxins

choices.label: E
choices.text: Transposons within the phage capsid translate the toxin directly

explanation.summary: Temperate bacteriophages often carry genes for toxins essential to bacterial virulence, such as diphtheria toxin.
explanation.whyCorrect: Temperate bacteriophages often contain DNA encoding proteins essential for bacterial virulence. The prime examples are bacterial toxins, including Shiga-like toxin, botulinum toxin, cholera toxin, erythrogenic toxin, and diphtheria toxin. A bacterium acquires the ability to make such a toxin when it is lysogenized by the phage carrying that gene.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Phages are viruses and do not divide by binary fission.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Transformation involves uptake of DNA, not preformed toxin protein, and this change followed phage infection.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Conjugation occurs between two bacteria through a sex pilus, not between a phage and a bacterium.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Transposons are DNA elements that relocate genes; they do not perform translation.

questions.stem: A medical student is reviewing the distribution of the human microbiota and is asked to identify the body site that harbors the greatest number of normal flora microbes in a healthy adult. Which of the following sites is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Colon

choices.label: B
choices.text: Lungs

choices.label: C
choices.text: Saliva

choices.label: D
choices.text: Skin

choices.label: E
choices.text: Stomach

explanation.summary: By far the highest concentration of normal flora is in the colon, which holds roughly 10^14 (10 to 100 trillion) microbes.
explanation.whyCorrect: Microbial density rises steeply as one descends the GI tract, and the colon carries approximately 10^14 organisms, mostly anaerobes. No other site approaches this number. The acidic stomach and the relatively nutrient-poor proximal small bowel hold far fewer organisms.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The upper lobes of the lungs are only lightly populated, with a few million microbes.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Saliva carries about 10^11 microbes, well below colonic numbers.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Skin carries about 10^11 microbes, three orders of magnitude fewer than the colon.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The stomach holds about 10^7 microbes because acid destroys most ingested organisms.

questions.topicName: Normal Flora: Role in Health and Disease

questions.stem: A healthy 30-year-old man undergoes a lecture demonstration in which cultures are taken from several body sites. Which of the following sites should be sterile in a healthy person?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Blood

choices.label: B
choices.text: Dental plaque

choices.label: C
choices.text: Ileum

choices.label: D
choices.text: Saliva

choices.label: E
choices.text: Vagina

explanation.summary: Blood, along with the central nervous system, heart, liver, spleen, bones, joints, and most internal organs, is normally sterile.
explanation.whyCorrect: Normal flora colonize surfaces that communicate with the outside world. Internal compartments such as the bloodstream are kept free of microbes, and the presence of organisms there represents dysbiosis or infection rather than normal colonization.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Dental plaque is one of the most densely colonized sites, with about 10^12 microbes.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The ileum carries about 10^11 microbes, including Lactobacillus and Bacteroides species.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Saliva carries about 10^11 microbes, including Streptococcus and Actinomyces species.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The vagina carries about 10^7 to 10^8 microbes, dominated by Lactobacillus species.

questions.topicName: Normal Flora: Role in Health and Disease

questions.stem: A 25-year-old woman undergoes a routine pelvic examination. Vaginal secretions are tested and the pH is 4.0. Which of the following best explains this finding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Candida species ferment glycogen into ethanol and acetate

choices.label: B
choices.text: Enterococcus species hydrolyze urea into ammonia and carbonate

choices.label: C
choices.text: Gardnerella species convert epithelial proteins into amines

choices.label: D
choices.text: Lactobacillus species ferment glycogen into lactic acid

choices.label: E
choices.text: Streptococcus species convert oxygen into hydrogen peroxide

explanation.summary: Lactobacillus species keep the vagina at a pH of about 4 by fermenting glycogen to lactic acid.
explanation.whyCorrect: Lactobacillus species dominate the vaginal flora and, as their name implies, generate lactic acid from glycogen supplied by the vaginal epithelium. Most microbes tolerate acid poorly, so this indirectly inhibits pathogens and prevents overgrowth of other normal flora.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Candida is a normal vaginal colonizer but is not the source of vaginal acidity.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Ammonia production would raise, not lower, the vaginal pH.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Amine release by Gardnerella produces the fishy odor of bacterial vaginosis, not a pH of 4.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Hydrogen peroxide generation by Streptococcus is not the mechanism taught for vaginal pH.

questions.topicName: Normal Flora: Role in Health and Disease

questions.stem: A 62-year-old postmenopausal woman is evaluated for recurrent vaginal discharge. Vaginal pH is 5.0. Which of the following best explains the change in her vaginal pH?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Chronic Candida colonization neutralizes the vaginal lactic acid

choices.label: B
choices.text: Declining estrogen reduces the glycogen available to Lactobacillus

choices.label: C
choices.text: Loss of Gardnerella allows colonization by acid-consuming anaerobes

choices.label: D
choices.text: Rising estrogen drives glycogen release and Lactobacillus overgrowth

choices.label: E
choices.text: Thinning of the vaginal wall increases local bicarbonate secretion

explanation.summary: Estrogen drives glycogen release from vaginal epithelium; as estrogen falls with age, Lactobacillus has less fuel for lactic acid and the pH rises toward 5.
explanation.whyCorrect: Estrogen promotes release of glycogen from the vaginal epithelium, and that glycogen is the substrate Lactobacillus ferments into lactic acid. With age, estrogen levels diminish, less lactic acid is produced, and vaginal pH approaches 5, increasing the risk of overgrowth of normal flora and infection by pathogens.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Candida overgrowth is a consequence of dysbiosis, not a cause of a rising vaginal pH.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Gardnerella is an opportunist that can overgrow when pH rises; its loss does not raise the pH.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Estrogen falls rather than rises after menopause, and more estrogen would lower rather than raise the pH.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Bicarbonate secretion by the atrophic vaginal wall is not the mechanism described for this change.

questions.topicName: Normal Flora: Role in Health and Disease

questions.stem: A physician explains to a patient that her vaginal pH has risen from 4 to 5. Compared with a pH of 4, a pH of 5 corresponds to which of the following changes in hydrogen ion concentration?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A 2-fold increase

choices.label: B
choices.text: A 5-fold increase

choices.label: C
choices.text: A 10-fold decrease

choices.label: D
choices.text: A 10-fold increase

choices.label: E
choices.text: A 100-fold decrease

explanation.summary: The pH scale is logarithmic, so a one-unit rise from 4 to 5 is a 10-fold decrease in hydrogen ion concentration.
explanation.whyCorrect: A shift in pH from 4 to 5 may look small, but because pH is logarithmic it means ten times fewer hydrogen ions. That loss of acidity meaningfully increases the risk of overgrowth of normal flora and infection by pathogenic microbes.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A doubling would correspond to a change of about 0.3 pH units, not a full unit.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A 5-fold change does not correspond to a one-unit shift on a base-10 logarithmic scale.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A rising pH means fewer, not more, hydrogen ions.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A 100-fold decrease corresponds to a two-unit rise, such as pH 4 to pH 6.

questions.topicName: Normal Flora: Role in Health and Disease

questions.stem: A newborn is delivered vaginally at term. Cultures taken from the infant shortly after birth are most likely to grow which of the following organisms?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bacteroides species

choices.label: B
choices.text: Corynebacterium species

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lactobacillus species

choices.label: D
choices.text: Propionibacterium species

choices.label: E
choices.text: Staphylococcus species

explanation.summary: Infants delivered vaginally initially acquire flora resembling the maternal vaginal flora, such as Lactobacillus species.
explanation.whyCorrect: Our symbiotic relationship with microbes begins at birth, and the route of delivery shapes the first flora acquired. Passage through the birth canal seeds the infant with vaginal organisms, of which Lactobacillus is the dominant member.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Bacteroides is a colonic anaerobe rather than a characteristic first colonizer at birth.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Corynebacterium is a skin organism acquired by infants delivered by cesarean section.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Propionibacterium is a skin organism typical of infants delivered by cesarean section.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Staphylococcus is a skin organism typical of infants delivered by cesarean section.

questions.topicName: Normal Flora: Role in Health and Disease

questions.stem: A term infant is delivered by cesarean section. During the first days of life, the infant's skin and gut are colonized with organisms resembling those of the primary caregiver's skin. Which of the following groups is most likely to be recovered?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Enterococcus, Escherichia, and Clostridium species

choices.label: B
choices.text: Lactobacillus, Bacteroides, and Bifidobacterium species

choices.label: C
choices.text: Staphylococcus, Corynebacterium, and Propionibacterium species

choices.label: D
choices.text: Streptococcus, Actinomyces, and Candida species

choices.label: E
choices.text: Veillonella, Fusobacterium, and Prevotella species

explanation.summary: Infants born by cesarean section first acquire flora that resembles the primary caregiver's skin flora.
explanation.whyCorrect: Because the infant does not pass through the birth canal, the earliest colonizers come from skin contact with caregivers. Staphylococcus, Corynebacterium, and Propionibacterium species are the characteristic skin organisms transferred in this way.

whyWrongByChoice.A: These organisms are members of the colonic flora rather than skin flora.
whyWrongByChoice.B: These organisms reflect vaginal and colonic flora, typical after vaginal delivery.
whyWrongByChoice.D: These are oral and salivary organisms rather than the skin flora of a caregiver.
whyWrongByChoice.E: These anaerobes are characteristic of dental plaque and saliva, not skin.

questions.topicName: Normal Flora: Role in Health and Disease

questions.stem: A 23-year-old woman completes a 10-day course of amoxicillin for sinusitis. Three days later she develops intense vulvar itching, swelling, and erythema with a thick white discharge, along with pain during intercourse and urination. Which of the following is the most likely cause of her symptoms?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Candida albicans

choices.label: B
choices.text: Clostridioides difficile

choices.label: C
choices.text: Gardnerella vaginalis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Lactobacillus species

choices.label: E
choices.text: Staphylococcus saprophyticus

explanation.summary: Antibiotics kill commensal bacteria and allow Candida albicans, a normal flora yeast, to overgrow and cause vulvovaginal candidiasis.
explanation.whyCorrect: C. albicans is a yeast that normally colonizes the oral, gastrointestinal, and vaginal tracts. Antibiotics cause dysbiosis by killing both pathogenic and commensal bacteria, allowing Candida to become dominant. Vulvovaginal candidiasis presents with intense itching, irritation, swelling, erythema, thick white discharge, dyspareunia, and dysuria.

whyWrongByChoice.B: C. difficile overgrowth after antibiotics causes colitis with watery diarrhea, not vaginitis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Gardnerella overgrowth causes bacterial vaginosis, which produces minimal inflammation and little pain.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Lactobacillus is the protective dominant flora that keeps the vagina acidic rather than a cause of vaginitis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: S. saprophyticus causes urinary tract infections, not a thick white vaginal discharge with vulvar erythema.

questions.topicName: Normal Flora: Role in Health and Disease

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman reports a thin greyish discharge coating the vaginal walls with a strong odor. She has minimal itching, burning, or pain, and the vulva appears uninflamed. Which of the following organisms most likely accounts for her presentation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Candida albicans

choices.label: B
choices.text: Escherichia coli

choices.label: C
choices.text: Gardnerella vaginalis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Lactobacillus species

choices.label: E
choices.text: Streptococcus species

explanation.summary: Bacterial vaginosis is commonly caused by overgrowth of Gardnerella vaginalis and presents with a thin, malodorous discharge and minimal inflammation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Overgrowth of vaginal bacteria produces bacterial vaginosis, most commonly attributed to Gardnerella vaginalis. Patients typically have a thin white or greyish discharge with a strong fishy smell from released amines, and unlike candidiasis the condition causes minimal inflammation and is usually not painful.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Candidiasis causes intense itching, swelling, erythema, and a thick white discharge.
whyWrongByChoice.B: E. coli is colonic flora and the leading cause of urinary tract infections, not this syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Lactobacillus is the protective dominant flora and does not cause a malodorous discharge.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Streptococcus species are normal vaginal colonizers but are not the cause of bacterial vaginosis.

questions.topicName: Normal Flora: Role in Health and Disease

questions.stem: A wet mount of vaginal secretions from a woman with a thin, malodorous discharge is reported as showing clue cells. Which of the following best describes a clue cell?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A ciliated columnar cell stripped of its surface microvilli

choices.label: B
choices.text: A neutrophil filled with ingested gram-negative diplococci

choices.label: C
choices.text: A squamous cell containing intracellular lactic acid granules

choices.label: D
choices.text: A squamous epithelial cell whose surface is coated with bacteria

choices.label: E
choices.text: A yeast cell bearing attached pseudohyphae and budding forms

explanation.summary: Clue cells are vaginal epithelial cells covered in bacteria and are used to diagnose bacterial vaginosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: On a stained preparation the flat, large, pink squamous epithelial cells are studded with small coccobacilli, which are Gardnerella vaginalis. The presence of these bacteria-coated epithelial cells is the finding used to make the diagnosis of bacterial vaginosis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Clue cells are squamous epithelial cells covered by bacteria, not damaged ciliated cells.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Intracellular diplococci within neutrophils are not the described basis for diagnosing bacterial vaginosis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Lactic acid is secreted by Lactobacillus into the environment and is not visible as intracellular granules.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Yeast with pseudohyphae points to candidiasis, a different diagnosis entirely.

questions.topicName: Normal Flora: Role in Health and Disease

questions.stem: Two women present to a clinic on the same day. The first has intense itching, swelling, erythema, and a thick white discharge. The second has a thin greyish discharge, little discomfort, and minimal inflammation. Which of the following features best distinguishes the second patient's condition from the first?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A history of recent antibiotic use preceding the symptoms

choices.label: B
choices.text: A thick, white, plaque-like discharge coating the vaginal walls

choices.label: C
choices.text: Marked inflammation and erythema of the vulvar tissues

choices.label: D
choices.text: More intense burning, itching, and dysuria on presentation

choices.label: E
choices.text: Release of amines producing a strong fishy odor

explanation.summary: Bacterial vaginosis is distinguished from vulvovaginal candidiasis by a thin malodorous discharge from released amines, with little inflammation or pain.
explanation.whyCorrect: Patients with bacterial vaginosis typically have less burning, itching, and dysuria than those with vulvovaginal candidiasis. Their thin, white or greyish discharge carries a strong fishy smell caused by the release of amines, and the condition usually produces minimal inflammation and little pain.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Antibiotic use is a recognized risk factor for both conditions, so it does not distinguish them.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A thick white discharge with plaque is the classic finding in vulvovaginal candidiasis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Marked inflammation and erythema characterize candidiasis; bacterial vaginosis has minimal inflammation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Burning, itching, and dysuria are more prominent in vulvovaginal candidiasis, not bacterial vaginosis.

questions.topicName: Normal Flora: Role in Health and Disease

questions.stem: A 4-month-old infant who recently finished a course of oral antibiotics is brought in with white plaques on the tongue and buccal mucosa. Which of the following organisms is the most likely cause?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Candida albicans

choices.label: B
choices.text: Clostridioides difficile

choices.label: C
choices.text: Gardnerella vaginalis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Moraxella catarrhalis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Staphylococcus epidermidis

explanation.summary: Thrush is an overgrowth of Candida species in the oral cavity, classically after antibiotic use, and presents as a white plaque.
explanation.whyCorrect: Candida albicans normally colonizes the oral cavity as part of the flora. Antibiotic use, birth control use, trauma, poorly fitting dentures, and immunosuppression allow it to overgrow, producing the characteristic white plaque of oral candidiasis. The name itself reflects the finding: Candida means white and albicans means to whiten.

whyWrongByChoice.B: C. difficile overgrowth after antibiotics causes colitis, not oral lesions.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Gardnerella overgrowth causes bacterial vaginosis rather than oral plaques.
whyWrongByChoice.D: M. catarrhalis is nasopharyngeal flora associated with acute otitis media.
whyWrongByChoice.E: S. epidermidis is a skin colonizer and does not form oral white plaques.

questions.topicName: Normal Flora: Role in Health and Disease

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man has white plaques in his mouth that scrape off. He takes no medications, has no dentures, has not received antibiotics, and reports no oral trauma. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Evaluate the patient's immune system with a CBC

choices.label: B
choices.text: Measure the salivary glycogen concentration

choices.label: C
choices.text: Obtain a stool culture for enteric bacterial pathogens

choices.label: D
choices.text: Screen household contacts for nasal carriage

choices.label: E
choices.text: Treat empirically with a broad-spectrum antibiotic

explanation.summary: Thrush without an obvious predisposing cause should prompt evaluation of the immune system.
explanation.whyCorrect: Thrush is typically triggered by antibiotic use, birth control use, trauma, poorly fitting dentures, or immunosuppression. When no obvious cause is apparent, the patient's immune system should be checked with a CBC, because thrush and other opportunistic infections can be a sign of a failing immune system.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Glycogen concentration is relevant to Lactobacillus in the vagina, not to oral thrush.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A stool culture evaluates enteric illness and does not explain unexplained oral candidiasis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Screening contacts for carriage addresses transmissible bacteria, not an endogenous opportunist.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Antibiotics kill bacteria and would worsen rather than treat Candida overgrowth.

questions.topicName: Normal Flora: Role in Health and Disease

questions.stem: A 2-year-old is brought in with ear pain and fever. Otoscopy shows a swollen, inflamed tympanic membrane with pus behind it. The three organisms that most commonly cause this infection are normal flora of which of the following sites?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Colon

choices.label: B
choices.text: Dental plaque

choices.label: C
choices.text: External auditory canal

choices.label: D
choices.text: Nasopharynx

choices.label: E
choices.text: Skin of the pinna

explanation.summary: Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, and Moraxella catarrhalis all reside as normal flora of the nasopharynx.
explanation.whyCorrect: The three most common causes of bacterial acute otitis media share one feature: they are nasopharyngeal normal flora. Disease occurs when these organisms migrate from the nasopharynx through the eustachian tube into the warm, moist middle ear, where they proliferate.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Colonic anaerobes do not migrate to the middle ear and are not implicated here.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Dental plaque anaerobes such as Veillonella and Prevotella are not causes of otitis media.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The external canal lies outside the tympanic membrane and is not the reservoir for these organisms.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Skin flora such as staphylococci and corynebacteria are not the common causes of otitis media.

questions.topicName: Normal Flora: Role in Health and Disease

questions.stem: A pediatrician explains to a parent why ear infections are frequent in toddlers but uncommon in adults. Which of the following anatomic features best accounts for this difference?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A larger tympanic membrane exposed to the outer ear canal

choices.label: B
choices.text: A longer and more vertical eustachian tube that traps fluid

choices.label: C
choices.text: A shorter, narrower, and more horizontal eustachian tube

choices.label: D
choices.text: A sterile nasopharynx that is readily colonized by skin flora

choices.label: E
choices.text: An absent mucociliary escalator within the middle ear cavity

explanation.summary: Children have a shorter, narrower, and more horizontal eustachian tube, which drains poorly and lets nasopharyngeal flora reach the middle ear.
explanation.whyCorrect: The child's eustachian tube geometry makes fluid drainage more difficult and makes it easier for normal flora to migrate from the nasopharynx into the middle ear. The smaller diameter also makes the tube more susceptible to blockage from inflammation or mucus, such as with upper respiratory infections or allergies.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Tympanic membrane size is not the described risk factor for acute otitis media in children.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A longer, more vertical tube describes the adult anatomy, which protects against otitis media.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The nasopharynx is not sterile; it normally harbors S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae, and M. catarrhalis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The difference taught is eustachian tube orientation and caliber, not a missing mucociliary escalator.

questions.topicName: Normal Flora: Role in Health and Disease

questions.stem: A 3-year-old is evaluated for possible acute otitis media. Which of the following sets of findings is most consistent with that diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Ear pain with a swollen, inflamed eardrum, pus, and fever

choices.label: B
choices.text: Painless white plaques on the tongue and hard palate

choices.label: C
choices.text: Thin grey vaginal discharge with a strong fishy odor

choices.label: D
choices.text: Watery diarrhea 10 to 15 times daily with abdominal cramping

choices.label: E
choices.text: Yellow-white pseudomembranes seen throughout the colon

explanation.summary: Acute otitis media presents with ear pain, swelling and inflammation of the tympanic membrane, pus in the ear, and a moderate fever.
explanation.whyCorrect: Migration of nasopharyngeal flora into the middle ear produces a warm, moist focus of infection. The resulting inflammation is seen on otoscopy as a swollen, erythematous tympanic membrane with pus behind it, accompanied by pain and moderate fever.

whyWrongByChoice.B: White oral plaques describe thrush, an overgrowth of Candida in the oral cavity.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A thin grey malodorous discharge describes bacterial vaginosis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Frequent watery diarrhea with cramping describes Clostridioides difficile infection.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Colonic pseudomembranes describe pseudomembranous colitis, not an ear infection.

questions.topicName: Normal Flora: Role in Health and Disease

questions.stem: A 2-month-old infant receives the Haemophilus influenzae type b and pneumococcal vaccines at a well-child visit. Which of the following best explains why these vaccines are given this early?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Encapsulated organisms cannot be cleared by any infant before 2 months

choices.label: B
choices.text: Infants are unable to mount an antibody response until after 6 months

choices.label: C
choices.text: Maternal IgA in breastmilk blocks vaccine responses before 2 months

choices.label: D
choices.text: Nasopharyngeal colonization by these organisms ceases after 2 months

choices.label: E
choices.text: Transplacental IgG declines by 3 to 6 months, leaving a vulnerable window

explanation.summary: Transplacental IgG wanes 3 to 6 months after birth, so vaccination at 2 months primes the infant's own antibody response before that protection is lost.
explanation.whyCorrect: Transplacental IgG serves as early immune protection against common, dangerous microbes, but these antibodies begin to diminish 3 to 6 months after birth. The gap between the loss of maternal antibody and the infant's own ability to respond is a critical period, and vaccination boosts the infant's immune response so that antibodies are present before exposure or loss of transplacental antibody.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The vaccine exists precisely because encapsulated strains cause invasive disease in older infants too.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Vaccination at 2 months works because infants can produce their own antibodies in response.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Breastmilk provides prebiotics and protection but is not described as blocking vaccine responses.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Carriage of these organisms in the nasopharynx does not stop at 2 months of age.

questions.topicName: Normal Flora: Role in Health and Disease

questions.stem: Two unvaccinated children in the same daycare are colonized in the nasopharynx with Streptococcus pneumoniae. One remains well while the other develops invasive disease. Which property of the colonizing strain best explains this difference?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Ability to ferment epithelial glycogen under anaerobic conditions

choices.label: B
choices.text: Formation of an adherent dental plaque biofilm on enamel

choices.label: C
choices.text: Possession of a polysaccharide capsule on the cell surface

choices.label: D
choices.text: Production of lactic acid that lowers the local mucosal pH

choices.label: E
choices.text: Secretion of a toxin that damages the colonic epithelium

explanation.summary: Encapsulated strains of nasopharyngeal flora are far more likely than unencapsulated strains to cause invasive disease.
explanation.whyCorrect: Some people carry S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae, and N. meningitidis as normal flora of the nasopharynx, and in some cases the strains carried are encapsulated. Encapsulated strains are much more likely to cause invasive disease than unencapsulated strains, which is why the childhood vaccines target these organisms.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Glycogen fermentation relates to vaginal Lactobacillus rather than nasopharyngeal invasion.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Plaque biofilm formation involves oral organisms such as S. mutans and does not drive invasion here.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Lactic acid production is a feature of Lactobacillus in the vagina, not of invasive pneumococci.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Toxin-mediated colonic damage describes C. difficile infection, not invasive pneumococcal disease.

questions.topicName: Normal Flora: Role in Health and Disease

questions.stem: A 19-year-old woman is airlifted to the emergency department after a severe car accident. Imaging and surgery reveal a lacerated colon with fecal matter spilled into the abdomen. She develops severe diffuse abdominal inflammation. Which of the following best explains this complication?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Entry of enormous numbers of microbes into a sterile cavity

choices.label: B
choices.text: Failure of colonization resistance within the vaginal tract

choices.label: C
choices.text: Loss of gastric acid allowing ingested pathogens to survive

choices.label: D
choices.text: Migration of nasopharyngeal flora through the eustachian tube

choices.label: E
choices.text: Overgrowth of a single opportunist within the colonic lumen

explanation.summary: Peritonitis follows spillage of trillions of colonic microbes into the normally sterile peritoneal cavity.
explanation.whyCorrect: The peritoneal cavity is normally sterile. When massive numbers of microbes from a lacerated colon enter it, the result is massive, life-threatening inflammation. Other emergencies such as a ruptured appendix, cancer, or obstruction can breach the GI tract the same way, and prompt surgical repair with cleaning of the cavity is critical.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Vaginal colonization resistance is unrelated to the abdominal findings after colonic laceration.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Gastric acid loss affects ingested organisms and does not explain diffuse peritoneal inflammation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Eustachian tube migration explains acute otitis media, not peritonitis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Luminal overgrowth of an opportunist describes conditions such as C. difficile colitis, not peritonitis.

questions.topicName: Normal Flora: Role in Health and Disease

questions.stem: A patient with a perforated colon develops infectious peritonitis. Before antimicrobial therapy is started, which of the following is the most common complication of this condition?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Acute otitis media

choices.label: B
choices.text: Bacterial vaginosis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Oral thrush

choices.label: D
choices.text: Pseudomembranous colitis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Septicemia

explanation.summary: Septicemia, a bloodstream infection, is a common complication of infectious peritonitis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Once trillions of microbes flood the peritoneal cavity, organisms readily spread into adjacent tissue and the bloodstream. This is why prompt surgical repair, washout of the cavity, and broad-spectrum antibiotics are used to eliminate any microbes that remain or are spreading.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Acute otitis media arises from nasopharyngeal flora reaching the middle ear, unrelated to peritonitis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Bacterial vaginosis results from vaginal dysbiosis and is not a complication of peritonitis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Thrush is a Candida overgrowth in the oral cavity, typically after antibiotics or immunosuppression.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Pseudomembranous colitis follows the broad-spectrum antibiotics used later, not the peritonitis itself.

questions.topicName: Normal Flora: Role in Health and Disease

questions.stem: A hospitalized patient who completed a month of broad-spectrum antibiotics develops watery diarrhea. Colonoscopy shows yellow-white pseudomembranes throughout the colon. Which of the following organisms is responsible?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Candida albicans

choices.label: B
choices.text: Clostridioides difficile

choices.label: C
choices.text: Gardnerella vaginalis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Staphylococcus aureus

choices.label: E
choices.text: Streptococcus pneumoniae

explanation.summary: Pseudomembranous colitis is caused by Clostridioides difficile, usually after antibiotic use.
explanation.whyCorrect: C. difficile, formerly called Clostridium difficile, is a member of the normal flora of the lower GI tract that is normally kept in check by other flora competing for space and food. After antibiotics remove that competition, it overgrows and its toxins damage the colonic lining, producing the yellow-white pseudomembranes seen at colonoscopy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Candida overgrowth produces thrush or vulvovaginal candidiasis, not colonic pseudomembranes.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Gardnerella overgrowth causes bacterial vaginosis and is not associated with colitis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: S. aureus causes skin infections, pneumonia, and sepsis rather than pseudomembranous colitis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: S. pneumoniae is nasopharyngeal flora associated with otitis media and invasive childhood disease.

questions.topicName: Normal Flora: Role in Health and Disease

questions.stem: A patient develops Clostridioides difficile colitis after a prolonged course of broad-spectrum antibiotics. Which of the following best explains how the antibiotics predisposed her to this infection?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Antibiotic binding to the toxin receptor on colonic epithelium

choices.label: B
choices.text: Antibiotic-driven increase in colonic mucus and secretory IgA

choices.label: C
choices.text: Direct antibiotic selection for capsule formation by the organism

choices.label: D
choices.text: Elimination of competing normal flora freed space and nutrients

choices.label: E
choices.text: Loss of gastric acid allowing ingested organisms to survive intact

explanation.summary: Broad-spectrum antibiotics cause dysbiosis by killing the normal flora that normally restrain C. difficile through competition.
explanation.whyCorrect: The number of C. difficile organisms is kept in check by other members of the normal flora competing for space and food. Antibiotic use kills off that normal flora, giving C. difficile the opportunity to spread and overgrow. This loss of colonization resistance is the same mechanism that allows other opportunists to emerge after antibiotics.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Antibiotics act on the bacteria themselves rather than by occupying a host toxin receptor.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Mucus and IgA production is a protective effect of intact normal flora, not of antibiotics.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Capsule expression drives invasive disease by nasopharyngeal flora, not antibiotic-associated colitis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Gastric acid is not the barrier discussed for C. difficile overgrowth in the lower GI tract.

questions.topicName: Normal Flora: Role in Health and Disease

questions.stem: A patient with Clostridioides difficile infection has watery diarrhea 10 to 15 times daily and becomes severely dehydrated. Which of the following best explains the volume of her diarrhea?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Destruction of goblet cells that eliminates the protective mucus layer

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fermentation of colonic glycogen into osmotically active lactic acid

choices.label: C
choices.text: Invasion of the bloodstream with systemic release of bacterial amines

choices.label: D
choices.text: Obstruction of the colonic lumen by a bulky adherent pseudomembrane

choices.label: E
choices.text: Toxin-mediated damage to the lining that impairs water absorption

explanation.summary: Toxins produced by C. difficile damage the GI lining, severely limiting water and nutrient absorption.
explanation.whyCorrect: Once C. difficile overgrows, the toxins it produces begin to damage the lining of the GI tract. That damage severely limits water and nutrient absorption, which is why patients may have watery diarrhea as often as 10 to 15 times a day, become extremely difficult to keep hydrated, and can develop kidney failure as a complication.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Loss of mucus alone is not the mechanism described for the fluid loss in this infection.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Glycogen fermentation to lactic acid is a vaginal Lactobacillus process, not a cause of colitis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Amine release explains the odor of bacterial vaginosis and does not cause watery diarrhea.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Pseudomembranes are a visible manifestation of mucosal damage rather than a cause of obstruction.

questions.topicName: Normal Flora: Role in Health and Disease

questions.stem: A patient treated with antibiotics for Clostridioides difficile infection improves, but her symptoms return shortly after each course ends. This cycle repeats several times. Which of the following best explains this pattern?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Antibiotics raise colonic glycogen levels that feed the residual organisms

choices.label: B
choices.text: She is reinfected by encapsulated strains carried in her own nasopharynx

choices.label: C
choices.text: The organism rapidly acquires plasmid-borne resistance during each course

choices.label: D
choices.text: The same antibiotics kill normal flora trying to reestablish their niche

choices.label: E
choices.text: Toxin persists in the colon for months after the organism has been cleared

explanation.summary: The antibiotics that cure C. difficile also kill the normal flora trying to return, setting up the next infection; 20 to 60% of patients are reinfected.
explanation.whyCorrect: Treating C. difficile with antibiotics is paradoxical: the same drugs that kill the organism also kill any normal flora attempting to reestablish their niche in the GI tract. Without restored colonization resistance, C. difficile overgrows again, and between 20 and 60% of treated patients become reinfected.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Colonic glycogen is not described as the substrate driving C. difficile recurrence.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Encapsulated nasopharyngeal strains cause invasive childhood disease, not recurrent colitis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The recurrence described is driven by absent normal flora rather than by acquired resistance.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Symptoms return because the organism regrows, not because toxin lingers after clearance.

questions.topicName: Normal Flora: Role in Health and Disease

questions.stem: A patient with repeated relapses of Clostridioides difficile infection is counseled about fecal microbiota transplantation. Approximately what proportion of patients make a full recovery and remain free of recurrent infection after the procedure?

choices.label: A
choices.text: About 50 to 60%

choices.label: B
choices.text: About 70 to 75%

choices.label: C
choices.text: About 80 to 85%

choices.label: D
choices.text: About 91 to 93%

choices.label: E
choices.text: About 99 to 100%

explanation.summary: Fecal transplantation cures roughly 91 to 93% of patients with recurrent C. difficile infection.
explanation.whyCorrect: Fecal transplants rapidly reestablish the patient's normal flora and thereby restore colonization resistance. The success of the procedure is very high, with around 91 to 93% of patients making a full recovery and remaining free of recurrent C. difficile infection, which makes it invaluable for patients who relapse after antibiotic therapy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: This substantially understates the reported success rate of the procedure.
whyWrongByChoice.B: This understates the reported success rate of fecal transplantation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: This is still below the reported success rate for the procedure.
whyWrongByChoice.E: No procedure is described as essentially universally curative for this infection.

questions.topicName: Normal Flora: Role in Health and Disease

questions.stem: A woman with recurrent Clostridioides difficile infection is scheduled for a fecal transplant using her mother as the donor. Which of the following is the most important step before the transplant is performed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Confirming that the donor and recipient share a blood type

choices.label: B
choices.text: Culturing the recipient's nasopharynx for encapsulated strains

choices.label: C
choices.text: Matching the donor and recipient by vaginal flora composition

choices.label: D
choices.text: Screening the donor stool sample for transmissible pathogens

choices.label: E
choices.text: Treating the donor with broad-spectrum antibiotics beforehand

explanation.summary: Donor stool must be screened for common pathogens so that dangerous microbes are not introduced into an already sick patient.
explanation.whyCorrect: For a fecal transplant, a donor stool sample is collected, mixed with saline, and liquefied before being introduced, typically via colonoscopy. Because the recipient is ill and the material is living microbiota, the sample must be screened for common pathogens to ensure dangerous microbes are not transferred.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Blood type compatibility is relevant to transfusion and organ transplant, not to fecal transplantation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Nasopharyngeal culture addresses respiratory colonizers unrelated to this procedure.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The transplant restores gastrointestinal flora; vaginal flora matching plays no role.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Antibiotics would destroy the donor's normal flora, which is the therapeutic component being transferred.

questions.topicName: Normal Flora: Role in Health and Disease

questions.stem: A student explains that gastrointestinal normal flora consume nutrients, occupy space, and produce acids, proteins, and fatty acids that directly impede other bacteria from growing. This obstruction to colonization by pathogens is best described by which of the following terms?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Colonization resistance

choices.label: B
choices.text: Dysbiosis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Opportunistic infection

choices.label: D
choices.text: Symbiosis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Transient colonization

explanation.summary: Colonization resistance is the obstruction to colonization by pathogens that is mediated by the microbiome.
explanation.whyCorrect: Once normal flora is established, a pathogen must overcome not only the immune system but also compete with resident microbes for space and resources. Members of the normal flora additionally produce acids, proteins, and fatty acids that actively impede other bacteria. This microbiome-mediated obstruction is termed colonization resistance.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Dysbiosis is an unhealthy change in the microbiota, the opposite of this protective effect.
whyWrongByChoice.C: An opportunistic infection is disease caused by flora under permissive conditions, not a defense.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Symbiosis describes flora that provide a benefit to the host, a broader concept than this mechanism.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Transient colonization refers to sporadic carriage of an organism that later disappears.

questions.topicName: Normal Flora: Role in Health and Disease

questions.stem: A physician explains that bacteria residing in the colon manufacture nutrients the host cannot make efficiently on its own. Which of the following do colonic bacteria produce?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Essential amino acids and absorbable heme iron

choices.label: B
choices.text: Vitamin A and long-chain polyunsaturated fats

choices.label: C
choices.text: Vitamin C and folate derived from dietary fiber

choices.label: D
choices.text: Vitamin D and calcium-binding transport proteins

choices.label: E
choices.text: Vitamin K, biotin, and certain B vitamins

explanation.summary: Colonic bacteria produce essential vitamins including vitamin K, biotin, and certain B vitamins.
explanation.whyCorrect: Beyond assisting with digestion and nutrient absorption, bacteria of the GI tract break down complex carbohydrates, proteins, and fats into simpler absorbable forms, and bacteria in the colon synthesize essential vitamins such as vitamin K, biotin, and several B vitamins that are vital to host metabolic processes.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Gut bacteria break down dietary protein but are not described as supplying essential amino acids or heme iron.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Vitamin A and long-chain fats are dietary in origin rather than products of colonic bacteria.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Vitamin C and folate are not the vitamins attributed to colonic bacterial synthesis here.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Vitamin D production depends on skin and host metabolism rather than colonic flora.

questions.topicName: Normal Flora: Role in Health and Disease

questions.stem: A researcher studies why intact gut flora reduces the likelihood that enteric microbes escape the GI tract and enter the bloodstream. Which of the following host effects of the normal flora best accounts for this?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Coating surface epithelial cells to convert them into clue cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: Increasing peristalsis so that microbes are flushed distally

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lowering the colonic pH below 4 by generating lactic acid

choices.label: D
choices.text: Producing a polysaccharide capsule that overlies the mucosa

choices.label: E
choices.text: Stimulating mucus, IgA, and tight junction protein production

explanation.summary: Gut flora stimulate goblet cell mucus, IgA and other immune proteins, and proteins that maintain tight junction integrity, all of which limit microbial escape.
explanation.whyCorrect: The normal flora of the GI tract induce mucus production from goblet cells, drive production of IgA and other immune proteins, and increase expression of proteins that maintain the integrity of the epithelial barrier. Together these changes decrease the likelihood that a microbe can escape the GI tract and enter the bloodstream.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Clue cells are bacteria-coated vaginal epithelial cells used to diagnose bacterial vaginosis.
